title: Ramadan and the Two Eids
objective: After this level you can explain why Muslims fast from dawn to sunset in Ramadan and what Eid al-Fitr and Eid al-Adha celebrate.
summary: In Ramadan Muslims fast from dawn to sunset to grow mindful of God; Eid al-Fitr ends the fast, and Eid al-Adha, at the height of the hajj, remembers Abraham's willingness to sacrifice his son.

cards.headline: A month without lunch, then one of Islam's two great festivals.
cards.body: Why do Muslims choose to go without food and water all day, and what do they celebrate when it's over?

cards.headline: Dawn to sunset
cards.body: Ramadan is the ninth month of the Islamic calendar. From dawn until sunset, Muslims who fast take no food or drink and abstain from sex. Children, the old, the ill, the disabled, travelers on long journeys, and pregnant or nursing women are exempt. Meals bookend the day: suhur before dawn, and after sunset the iftar, which usually begins with dates, as was Muhammad's custom.

cards.headline: Why fast?
cards.body: The Quran says fasting is prescribed so that believers may become mindful of God. Muslims also describe it as training in self-discipline and a way to share the hunger of the poor. It isn't only about food: false words or bad deeds are held to spoil a fast as much as eating. And the month has a birthday. Muslims believe the Quran's revelation began on one of Ramadan's last ten nights in 610, Laylat al-Qadr, the Night of Power.

cards.headline: Two Eids
cards.body: Eid al-Fitr, the "Feast of Fast-Breaking", ends Ramadan: new clothes for children, prayers at the mosque, gifts and family meals, and thanks to God for the strength to keep the fast. Eid al-Adha, the "Festival of Sacrifice", begins on the 10th of Dhu al-Hijjah, at the height of the hajj. It remembers the story, as Muslims tell it, of Abraham's willingness to sacrifice his son Ishmael, who was replaced by a ram. Families sacrifice an animal and share the meat with the poor, relatives and friends.

mascot.line: People mix up the two Eids. Fitr ends the Ramadan fast; Adha, the sacrifice, comes with the hajj.

cards.headline: Ramadan and the Two Eids: the takeaways
learned: Muslims fast from dawn to sunset in Ramadan, with exemptions
They believe the Quran's revelation began in Ramadan
Eid al-Fitr ends the fast; Eid al-Adha remembers Abraham's sacrifice

questions.prompt: Match each Ramadan and Eid name with its meaning or time.
questions.explanation: Eid al-Fitr is the Feast of Fast-Breaking and Eid al-Adha the Festival of Sacrifice. Laylat al-Qadr is the Night of Power, and suhur is the meal before dawn.

questions.prompt: How do Muslims who fast in Ramadan structure each day?

options.label: They eat one big meal at noon and then fast through the whole night
options.rationale: The fast runs from dawn to sunset, not through the night.

options.label: They fast every other day of the month
options.rationale: The fast is kept every day of the month.

options.label: They give up meat but keep their usual meals
options.rationale: No food or drink at all during daylight.

options.label: They eat suhur before dawn, fast, then break the fast at sunset

questions.explanation: Suhur comes before dawn, the fast lasts until sunset, and the iftar, often starting with dates, breaks it.

questions.prompt: Muslims date the first revelation on Mount Hira to 610. How does Ramadan remember it?

options.label: Muslims believe it began on one of Ramadan's last ten nights
Ramadan begins on the anniversary of the hijra
options.rationale: The hijra was a different event, in 622.

options.label: The fast ends on the day Muhammad was born
options.rationale: Eid al-Fitr ends the fast; it isn't a birthday.

options.label: Pilgrims climb up to Mount Hira's cave on the last night of the fast
options.rationale: No climb is tied to the fast; the revelation is remembered on the Night of Power.

questions.explanation: Muslims believe the revelation began on Laylat al-Qadr, the Night of Power, one of the last ten nights of Ramadan in 610.
